findings.title: Shipped oracleMaxSpotDeviationBps = 50 is below the basis this repo itself measured on Unichain; the mandatory pre-deploy recalibration is absent from the runbook and the justifying comment cites only the quiet snapshot
findings.location: script/chain_params.json:18,44,101,117,154; script/DeployStableLP.s.sol:57-60; script/RUNBOOK-2026-09-05.md (Предпосылки / per-chain checklist, :161-162); tasks/oracle_maxdeviation_analysis.md snapshot 2
findings.body:
`_checkSpot` computes `|poolPrice − refPrice| / refPrice` in bps and compares it against `maxSpotDeviationBps` (src/oracle/ChainlinkPriceOracle.sol:289-297). That is byte-for-byte the same quantity `script/PriceDeviation.s.sol` tabulates as "basis" — I verified the three expressions (`mulDiv(sqrtP,sqrtP,Q96)`, the decimal-adjusted pool price, the two-feed cross) match the script's `_v4Price`/`_chainlinkPrice`. So the repo's own basis table is directly comparable to the shipped tolerance.

The branch ships `"oracleMaxSpotDeviationBps": 50` explicitly on chains 1, 130, 8453, 42161 and 1301, and every other chain entry in `chain_params.json` carries `"oracle": true` and inherits the same 50 from `DEFAULT_ORACLE_MAX_SPOT_DEVIATION_BPS`. `tasks/oracle_maxdeviation_analysis.md` snapshot 2 (2026-07-21) records **Unichain ETH/UNI basis 72 bps and ETH/WBTC 39 bps** — 72 is above the shipped tolerance on a calm day, and 39 leaves 11 bps. This is not a transient: the same document diagnoses the cause as Unichain's 18-decimal SVR proxies on a 24 h heartbeat, and `script/oracle_feeds.json` chain 130 confirms `heartbeat: 87300` on every feed, so a day-lagged answer still passes `_read`'s freshness test and reaches the deviation compare. The oracle therefore asserts a stale reference and reverts `SpotPriceOutOfBounds`, rather than declining with `false`.

Consequence: on a manager configured with a Unichain ETH/UNI (or similarly lagged) pool, every operator `allocate`, `allocateFrom`, `reinvest`, `recenter` and `moveLiquidity` reverts for as long as the basis is out of band. This is a liveness failure only — `_guardSwap` returns immediately for `byOwner` (src/BaseLPManager.sol:355), so the NFT owner can allocate, recenter, move and withdraw throughout, and `claimFees` is not gated on either product. It reaches only managers created from the new implementations; existing clones are unaffected.

Several quantitative claims that circulated during this audit do **not** hold and should not be carried into a decision: mainnet and Arbitrum sit comfortably inside 50 in the measured data (mainnet worst 33 on ETH/WBTC 0.05%, Arbitrum worst 26 on the thin ARB/USDC 0.30% pool), and the theory that "basis tracks the fee tier" is contradicted by the same table (mainnet ETH/USDC 0.30% = 16 vs ETH/USDC 0.05% = 20; USDC/cbBTC 0.30% = 3). The driver is feed lag, which is per-feed and per-chain, not per-tier — which matters because it determines the right remedy.

Two process defects sit on top of the number. First, `tasks/task_053_operator_add_spot_guard.md:80-81` makes re-running `script/PriceDeviation.s.sol` across four chains and taking a **high percentile, not one snapshot** an explicit pre-deploy precondition; `script/RUNBOOK-2026-09-05.md` — the document that actually gets executed — contains no mention of `PriceDeviation`, basis or percentile anywhere (verified by grep), and its post-deploy check at :162 merely asserts `maxSpotDeviationBps() == 50`. Second, the comment justifying the constant (`script/DeployStableLP.s.sol:57-59`) says "Live basis was 0-3 bps on stable pairs and ~33 bps on ETH/WBTC when `PriceDeviation.s.sol` was last run" — snapshot 1 numbers attributed to the last run, when snapshot 2 is the last run on record and contains the readings that break the choice. It also drops the ETH majors from the very snapshot it cites (mainnet ETH/USDC 20, ETH/USDT 24), so it reads as more reassuring than its own source supports. `script/README.md:196` repeats the same narrow citation. A future maintainer sizing this parameter is pointed at exactly the subset of the data that fits.
findings.recommendation: Before broadcasting: (1) add the task's own precondition to `script/RUNBOOK-2026-09-05.md` Предпосылки — re-run `script/PriceDeviation.s.sol` on the four measurable chains over a volatile window and set the tolerance from a high percentile; (2) set `oracleMaxSpotDeviationBps` **per chain** in `chain_params.json` (the plumbing at DeployStableLP.s.sol:322-326 already supports it) rather than one global 50; (3) for chain 130 specifically, either raise it above the measured percentile or follow the analysis document's own conclusion (:91-93) and keep BTC/UNI pools out of the operator-managed set there — note the fix converts "don't rely on this oracle for BTC/UNI" into "operators cannot touch BTC/UNI", which is a change of meaning neither the task nor the runbook records; (4) correct DeployStableLP.s.sol:57-59 and script/README.md:196 to cite the 2026-07-21 snapshot and its worst readings. Zero manager bytes — config, docs and one oracle constructor argument. Recoverable post-deploy in one owner transaction (`setMaxSpotDeviationBps`, capped at MAX_DEVIATION_CAP = 1000), and per-manager via `setPriceOracle` to a differently-tuned oracle instance, so this blocks the chain-130 oracle parameter rather than the whole run.

findings.title: A freshly created manager is born with priceOracle == 0, which now means its operator can do nothing at all — and there is no init parameter, no factory wiring, and no Stable UI to fix it
findings.body:
`priceOracle` is not in either product's `InitParams` (verified: StableLPManager.sol:50-55, VolatileLPManager.sol:39-44) and is written only by the `onlyOwnerNFT` setter at BaseLPManager.sol:332; `script/CreateManager.s.sol` does not call it. So every clone minted from the new implementations starts with `priceOracle == address(0)`.

Before this fix that state meant "operators can manage liquidity, they just cannot swap". After it, `StableLPManager._addLiquidity:215` and `VolatileLPManager._addLiquidityAt:288` call `_guardSwap(byOwner, key, true, 0, 0)` on every add, so a zero oracle reverts `OperatorSwapGuardRequired` on `allocate`, `allocateFrom`, `reinvest`, `recenter` and `moveLiquidity`. The delegated-bot product — the entire point of the operator role — is inert on every new manager until the owner sends one extra transaction that nothing in the creation flow prompts.

On Stable the gap has no in-app remedy at all: `OracleSection` is the only UI that calls `setPriceOracle` and it is rendered under `{isVol && ...}` (operators/page.tsx:155), even though the hook behind it already writes with `StableLPManagerAbi`. Worse, `stablelp-ui/src/lib/errors.ts:9` renders `OperatorSwapGuardRequired` as "The owner can set one under Oracle" — pointing a Stable owner at a card their product never renders. The owner's fallbacks are a block-explorer write tab or `cast send`.

Scope and bound: no funds are at risk or stuck (the owner bypasses the guard entirely and `withdrawTo` is `onlyOwnerNFT`), `claimFees` still works for operators, existing clones are unaffected, and one owner transaction fixes it permanently. The severity comes from it hitting *every* manager created after this deploy, on the product's headline feature, with a broken in-app remedy on one of the two products. `script/RUNBOOK-2026-09-05.md` post-deploy item 5 opens a frontend task for task_053 and item 6 states the new feed-coverage precondition, but neither names the `isVol` render gate or the born-oracle-less default.
findings.recommendation: Before announcing new-manager creation on the new implementations: (a) drop the `isVol &&` gate at operators/page.tsx:155 so `OracleSection` renders for both products, and reword errors.ts:9 (one-line changes in the sibling repo, zero contract bytes); (b) promote both to blocking items in the runbook's post-deploy list rather than polish; (c) have `CreateManager.s.sol` — and the UI's create flow — set the protocol default oracle immediately after `initialize`, so the manager is never handed over inert. Adding an oracle field to `InitParams` would be the cleanest fix but is the only option with a byte cost: it touches both products and would have to be measured against VolatileLPManager's 197 B (spent twice, since OpenVolatileLPManager carries its own 257 B budget); I do not recommend it for this run. Does not block the contract deploy.

findings.title: The documented residual omits the pool-vs-feed basis, and the README's sizing rule is unsatisfiable and wrong in the loosening direction
findings.body:
Three documents state the post-fix residual as extraction within `maxSpotDeviationBps − poolFee` per operation. The guard, however, bounds the pool against the **Chainlink reference**, not against the price the pool reverts to. Writing the reference as `market·(1+b)`, an attacker choosing the sign that helps reaches `|b| + D` of mispricing, so the correct expression is `basis + maxSpotDeviationBps − poolFee`. The repo measured `b` at 16-33 bps on the mainnet pools and 26-72 bps on Arbitrum/Unichain, so the documented figure understates the accepted residual by roughly 1.7x on mainnet ETH/WBTC 0.05% (78 vs 45 bps) and up to ~4.6x on Unichain ETH/UNI 0.30% (92 vs 20 bps). This is a magnitude correction to a residual the task already accepts as deliberate and repeatable — it does not open a new path, and it leaves per-operation exposure well under 1% of redeployed principal on the configured mainnet set, versus the PoC's −22.4%/−44.5%.

The part that will cause a future mistake is `script/README.md:196`: "a spot tolerance at or above the fee tier of the thinnest configured pool gives the guard nothing to do". With the basis term restored, zero residual requires `D < poolFee − basis`, which is negative on every configured pool whose basis exceeds its fee tier — mainnet ETH/WBTC (33 vs 5), ETH/USDT (24 vs 5), WBTC/USDC (17 vs 5), Unichain ETH/UNI (72 vs 30). No positive tolerance eliminates the residual on those pools; the guard bounds it, it cannot remove it. The rule as written tells a deployer that a sub-fee-tier tolerance would make the guard airtight, and simultaneously implies that anything above the fee tier is pointless — a reading that would encourage either an unsatisfiably tight setting (which fail-closes all operator activity) or dismissing the guard entirely. Both are wrong: at the shipped 50 bps on a 30 bps pool the guard still cuts the PoC's drain from ~4450 bps to ~20-90 bps per operation. The same paragraph is the sizing guidance the deployer will read alongside F-1's number.

Relatedly, `tasks/task_053_operator_add_spot_guard.md:77-79` argues "at 50 bps on a 0.30% pool ~0.2% remains, on a 1% pool the attack is unprofitable". With the basis folded in, the unprofitability conclusion flips wherever `b > 50` — a value the repo measured on Unichain. That is a qualitative error in the fix's own profitability argument, not just a magnitude one.
findings.recommendation: Doc-and-parameter work only; zero manager bytes. (1) State the residual as `basis + maxSpotDeviationBps − poolFee` in script/README.md:193-195, task_053 and the CHANGELOG. (2) Replace the fee-tier rule at README:196 with the sizing rule that actually applies: the tolerance must exceed a high percentile of the measured basis of the widest configured pool (or operator ops fail closed), the residual it leaves cannot be driven to zero on any pool whose basis exceeds its fee tier, and the guard's job is to kill the 20-80% skews, not to police the last 50 bps. (3) Correct the task's "unprofitable on a 1% pool" claim. (4) Optionally add a per-pool tolerance override on the oracle (`mapping(PoolId => uint16)` + owner setter, ~150-300 B on a contract with 18,675 B of margin, 0 B in any manager) so stable pairs can run at 10-20 bps while a lagged pair runs wider. Does not block, but ship the doc corrections in the same commit as the parameter decision from F-1.

findings.title: The guard's meaning changed but every documentation surface outside the diff still says "swap" — including advice that would brick an owner's manager — and UniLens, redeployed in this very run, does not expose maxSpotDeviationBps
findings.body:
`git diff master..HEAD -- src` touches exactly three files: StableLPManager.sol, VolatileLPManager.sol and oracle/ChainlinkPriceOracle.sol. `src/interfaces/IPriceOracle.sol`, `src/BaseLPManager.sol` and `src/UniLens.sol` are untouched, and all three still describe a swap-only guard.

**The interface.** `tasks/task_053_operator_add_spot_guard.md:112` mandated this edit verbatim ("`IPriceOracle.sol` does not change: only the natspec is edited — `amountIn == 0` means spot-check"). It was not made. The interface still says `check` is "called right after each swap" and documents `amountIn` as "the input amount paid to the pool", with no sentinel. `setPriceOracle` accepts any address and performs no capability probe (BaseLPManager.sol:331-333). A second `IPriceOracle` written against the published contract has **undefined** behaviour on `check(key, true, 0, 0)`: an implementation modelled on this repo's expected-output arithmetic computes `expectedOut = 0`, `minOut = 0`, `0 < 0` is false and returns `true` — every operator add vouched for unconditionally, H-1 fully reinstated; one that guards its inputs or computes `amountOut/amountIn` literally returns false or panics — every operator add bricked. Master's own oracle chose the fail-closed branch with an explicit `|| amountIn == 0 ⇒ return false` clause, which is precisely the clause a third-party implementer has no reason to write. Note this is not purely hypothetical across the deploy: a new-implementation manager pointed at an **already-deployed master-version** oracle fail-closes on every add. The runbook anticipates that (:130-138, ordering: oracle before implementations) but the code carries no signal.

**The manager.** Three BaseLPManager natspec blocks now misdescribe live behaviour, one of them harmfully. `:138-142` on the `priceOracle` field: "External price guard for **operator-triggered** on-chain swaps ... Zero ⇒ operators cannot swap at all". `:183-185` on the event: "zero ⇒ operators cannot swap". `:327-330` on the setter: "The oracle gates **operator** swaps only; clearing it (zero) does not weaken the owner but disables operator-triggered swaps entirely" — an owner who suspects a mis-fed oracle and follows that sentence to `setPriceOracle(0)` will discover their bot cannot add liquidity at all, on either product. And `:342-350`, `_guardSwap`'s own header, still opens "Economic-safety guard for a just-executed swap" and enumerates its call sites as "(Stable `allocate`/`reinvest` pre-swaps, Volatile `allocate`/`recenter`)" — naming no add path and no sentinel. That is the comment a maintainer reads before refactoring `_addLiquidity`/`_addLiquidityAt`; as written it presents the two new `(…, true, 0, 0)` calls as misplaced.

**The lens.** `UniLens` is deployed in this run on chains 1, 130, 8453, 42161 and 1301 (`"lens": true`), has 10,044 B of headroom, and is the surface the bot and UI read to predict a guard failure. `OracleStatus` (:120-129) carries `maxDeviationBps` and no `maxSpotDeviationBps`; `oracleStatus` (:200-235) never reads it (grep confirms the identifier does not appear in the file). Its natspec repeats the swap-only framing ("`oracle == address(0)` ⇒ operators cannot swap at all", "Operator swaps are fail-closed"). So nothing off-chain can predict a `SpotPriceOutOfBounds`, and the field that F-1 shows is the operationally decisive one is invisible to the tooling — on the one deploy where adding it is free.

Also in this class, at INFO weight: the errors themselves are swap-named (`OperatorSwapGuardRequired`, `OperatorSwapUnverified(PoolId)`) and now fire on swapless paths. Renaming them costs zero runtime bytes but breaks the ABI shared with already-deployed managers and the frontend's matcher, so it should be decided now or never — I recommend never, and fixing the prose instead.
findings.recommendation: One documentation edit set plus one lens field, all before broadcast. Natspec (zero runtime bytes, no EIP-170 impact): (a) `IPriceOracle.check` — state that `amountIn == 0` is a mandatory spot-price question about `key`, that `zeroForOne` is meaningless in that branch, that an implementation which cannot answer it MUST return `false` and must never return `true` vacuously, and that the implementation needs its own PoolManager reference; (b) BaseLPManager :138-142, :183-185, :327-330 and :342-350 — say the oracle gates every operator value-moving operation, swaps and liquidity adds alike, and that clearing it disables operators outright rather than merely their swaps; (c) UniLens :105-129 and :190-196 likewise. Lens field: add `uint16 maxSpotDeviationBps` to `OracleStatus` and a `try o.maxSpotDeviationBps()` probe in `oracleStatus` — roughly 60-120 B against 10,044 B of headroom, 0 B in any manager. Doing it in this run avoids a second lens deploy and a second ABI sync on the frontend.

findings.title: The fail-closed surface widened past what the docs disclose: no-feed pools, a cheap third-party skew, and the L2 sequencer grace period now stop operator liquidity ops, not just swaps
findings.body:
`script/README.md:180-190` documents two consequences of the widening — a pool with no feed becomes entirely operator-inert, and a market move outrunning the heartbeat blocks operator ops until the feed catches up — and calls the second the intended trade. Two further consequences are not disclosed.

**The sequencer gate now governs liquidity.** `check` opens with `if (!_sequencerUp()) return false` (:227), and `_sequencerUp` (:326-334) requires the uptime feed to read "up" **and** `block.timestamp - startedAt > sequencerGracePeriod`, defaulted to 3600 s. Before this fix that gate only stopped operator swaps; now, on Base and Arbitrum, for a full hour after any sequencer restart every operator `allocate`, `reinvest`, `recenter` and `moveLiquidity` reverts `OperatorSwapUnverified` — which is exactly the window after a restart in which positions are most likely to have drifted out of range. Fail-closed is the right default here, but it is a new operational property on the two chains that have an operator running, and it appears in no runbook or README line.

**Third-party griefing is cheaper than before.** Any account that pushes a configured pool more than `maxSpotDeviationBps` off the reference denies every operator liquidity op in that pool until ordinary flow or a feed update closes the gap. This existed for swap-bearing operator legs since task_031; it now covers swapless `recenter`, `moveLiquidity`, `allocate` and `reinvest`, which previously had no price precondition at all (the branch's own inverted tests pin the change: `test_operatorSwaplessRecenter_noOracle_succeeds` → `_reverts`). Persistence is bounded, contrary to how this is sometimes stated: arbitrage is priced against the market and pays the fee once, so only a nudge no larger than the pool's own fee tier is free to hold — which requires the standing basis to have already consumed most of the tolerance, i.e. the F-1 condition. The attacker profits nothing (a reverted operator tx yields nothing extractable) and must keep paying to hold it. The operator also has an in-transaction remedy on the swap-bearing paths: a corrective pre-swap in the same pool executes better than the reference-implied price and clears the 100 bps swap gate by construction, unblocking its own add.

Bound on all of it: the NFT owner bypasses the guard entirely (BaseLPManager.sol:355) and can allocate, recenter, move and `withdrawTo` at any time; `claimFees` is ungated on both products; nothing is stuck or seizable. The loss is operator automation and the yield foregone while a drifted position goes unrecentered.
findings.recommendation: Add both to `script/README.md`'s consequence list (:183-190) and to the runbook: an L2 sequencer restart suspends all operator liquidity operations for `sequencerGracePeriod`, and a pool can be pushed into an operator-inert state by anyone at roughly the round-trip fee when the standing basis is close to the tolerance — the remedy being an owner transaction or waiting out the gap. Sizing the tolerance off a percentile (F-1) rather than a quiet snapshot is what makes the griefing push cost real money instead of a few bps. Zero bytes anywhere.

findings.title: The Stable half of the fix is not pinned by any test: two independent mutations that reopen H-1 on Stable leave all 293 tests green
findings.body:
`MockPriceOracle.Mode.RejectSpot` was added by this change for exactly one purpose, stated in its own natspec (test/helpers/Mocks.sol:65-68): "`check` is `view`, so the mock cannot count calls, and a mock that ignores its arguments would let the guard be refactored away unnoticed." `grep -rn RejectSpot test/` returns only the mock and two Volatile tests (VolatileLPManagerOperatorSwapGuard.t.sol:239,248). There is no Stable use, and no Stable manager test anywhere wires the real `ChainlinkPriceOracle` through an add path — the new PoC (test/Audit20260904SwaplessDrainPoC.t.sol) imports `VolatileLPManager` only.

Two concrete mutations survive the suite. **(a) Wrong sentinel argument.** Change StableLPManager.sol:215 to `_guardSwap(byOwner, key, true, 1, 0)`. All nine Stable guard tests still pass: `Mode.Pass` returns true for any argument, `NotEnforced` returns false for any argument, `Revert` reverts regardless, and the no-oracle cases revert in `_guardSwap` before `check` is reached. Against the real oracle the mutated call takes the *swap* branch, where for an equal-decimal pair `expectedOut` and `minOut` both round to 0 and `0 < 0` is false — the plumbing stays intact (a missing or stale feed still fails closed) while the price comparison becomes unconditionally satisfied. **(b) Guard bypassed on reinvest.** Change the `byOwner` threaded into `_addLiquidity` at StableLPManager.sol:308 to a hardcoded `true`. Every operator reinvest test carries a swap — `_reinvestLeg()` is `_swapLeg()[0]` with `swapAmountIn: 100e18` (test/StableLPManagerOperatorSwapGuard.t.sol:70-88), and the in-bounds case sets `swapAmountIn = 1e6` — so the revert they observe comes from the pre-existing swap guard at :298, never from the new add guard; every other `reinvest` caller in the suite (`grep -rn '\.reinvest(' test/`) runs as `owner`, which bypasses by design. There is also no Stable `..._notEnforcedOracle_reverts` case, which Volatile has at :205.

One further gap, on the interaction rather than the wiring: no non-fork test exercises a price-moving pre-swap followed by a spot-checked add at the deployed tolerance. `test/GasCompareVolatile.fork.t.sol:405` does combine `swapAmountIn: 0.1e18` with a real oracle, but it is `BASE_RPC`-gated (a silent no-op in default CI) and builds the oracle with a 500 bps spot tolerance — 10x the deployed default — and the adjacent case at :469 explicitly opts out of the spot branch. So the swap-then-add interaction at 50 bps is unpinned everywhere.

Impact bound: a silent regression on Stable is materially smaller than on Volatile. Stable's ranges are set once at `initialize` and have no setter (src/StableLPManager.sol:58-60,78, verified), and its operator surface is `allocate`/`allocateFrom`/`reinvest`/`claimFees` with no principal-removal path — so an operator there cannot open a narrow band at a skewed price or recycle principal. The exposure is idle balance plus realized fees deployed at a bad price into a fixed range, not the −22%/−44% principal drain the Volatile PoC showed.
findings.recommendation: Tests only, zero bytes. Add to test/StableLPManagerOperatorSwapGuard.t.sol: (1) `test_operatorSwaplessAllocate_consultsTheOracleOnSpot` — `Mode.RejectSpot`, operator allocate with `swapAmountIn == 0`, expect `MockSpotChecked` (kills mutation a); (2) `test_operatorSwaplessReinvest_consultsTheOracleOnSpot` — `_accrueFees()` first, operator reinvest with `swapAmountIn == 0` (kills mutation b); (3) the missing `..._notEnforcedOracle_reverts`. Then one non-fork test pinning the swap-then-add interaction at the deployed 50 bps against a real `ChainlinkPriceOracle` + `MockAggregator`. Strongest addition, if the budget allows: a Stable arm of test/Audit20260904SwaplessDrainPoC.t.sol, which is also the cheapest way to answer whether Stable needs the gate's availability cost at all.

findings.title: The documented remediation for a stale circuit-breaker cache is a no-op: SetOracleFeeds skips exactly the case a Chainlink phase change produces, and a test pins the skip as correct
findings.body:
`setFeed` is the only writer of `feedBounds`, and its natspec says: "Chainlink can swap the aggregator behind a proxy (a phase change), which leaves the cache stale — re-run `SetOracleFeeds` after one." But `applyFeeds` skips a currency whose stored `(aggregator, heartbeat, tokenDecimals)` already matches (script/SetOracleFeeds.s.sol:85-89), and a phase change swaps the underlying aggregator *behind* the registered proxy, leaving all three identical. The prescribed refresh prints "skip (current)" and writes nothing. `test/SetOracleFeeds.t.sol` asserts the skip as desired behaviour, so the gap is actively pinned.

The skip tuple is wrong on two cached values, not one: `setFeed` also caches `feedDecimals` from `IAggregatorV3(aggregator).decimals()` (:162), which is a *pricing* input to both the swap branch (:262-263) and `_checkSpot` (:293). A phase change that moved decimals would silently mis-scale every comparison with the same no-op remediation. Chainlink keeps decimals stable across phases, so that half is theoretical; the bounds half is not.

Direction of harm, corrected from how this was first framed: Chainlink has deprecated min/maxAnswer on most feeds, and mainnet USDC currently reports the `2^176 − 1` sentinel (which `_readBounds` correctly drops as "no bound" because it exceeds `int128.max`), while Base/Arbitrum USDC still carry a legacy 1.05e8 ceiling. The plausible pending migration is therefore bounded → unbounded, which leaves the cache *tighter* than reality and fails **closed** — an operator add reverting during a >5% depeg. The fail-open direction (a stale zero bound while a new breaker is added) requires Chainlink to reverse its own deprecation, plus a depeg that pins the feed, plus a compromised operator, and would only return the oracle to its pre-fix state (audit L-3, rated LOW). Either way this is a hole in a defence-in-depth mitigation, not a live exploit.

The contract is not stuck: the oracle owner can refresh at any time with a direct `setFeed(currency, sameAggregator, sameHeartbeat, sameDecimals)`, which recomputes bounds unconditionally. Only the *documented* path cannot do it, and neither `script/README.md` nor the runbook mentions bounds at all.
findings.recommendation: Pick one, both cheap and both outside the EIP-170 budget. Either make `applyFeeds` compare `oracle.feedBounds(currency)` (and `feedDecimals`) against a fresh read of the resolved aggregator, or honour a `FORCE=1` env that disables the skip — and update test/SetOracleFeeds.t.sol accordingly. Alternatively add an owner-only `refreshBounds(Currency[])` to the oracle (~150-250 B against 18,675 B of headroom) and point the natspec at it. In every case correct the comment at ChainlinkPriceOracle.sol:156-157: as written it sends an operator down a path that provably does nothing. Does not block.

findings.title: The oracle's sentinel-safety comment asserts an invariant StableLPManager._handleReinvest does not hold
findings.body:
The comment that justifies the `amountIn == 0` sentinel — added by this branch — reads: "What makes the sentinel safe is that no real swap can wear it, guarded twice over: the swap paths reach `_guardSwap` only inside `if (swapAmountIn > 0)`, and what they pass is the *realized* input, which their full-fill check has already required to be no smaller than the requested one."

Of the three swap-path `_guardSwap` invocations, two carry the full-fill check (`StableLPManager:189`, `VolatileLPManager:224`, the latter shared by allocate, recenter and move) and one does not: `_handleReinvest` swaps at :294 and guards at :298 with no `SwapSlippage` revert between them. A zero realized input is reachable there without a revert — a hookless Stable pool whose price has drifted outside the manager's fixed range, with no other liquidity between spot and the operator-chosen `swapPriceLimit`, lets `SwapMath.computeSwapStep` walk the price to the limit consuming nothing — so half of the stated double guard is absent at that site.

The consequence today is benign: `inDelta == 0` implies `outDelta == 0` (nothing moved), the swap branch would be vacuous at zero magnitude anyway (`expectedOut = 0`, `minOut = 0`), and the check the call receives instead — `_checkSpot` — is symmetric and, at the shipped 100/50 configuration, tighter than the one it displaces. Note that last point is a deployment convention rather than a code invariant: both tolerances are independently owner-settable against the same 1000 bps cap, so an inverted configuration would make the sentinel path the weaker of the two and remove the accident that makes this harmless.

The defect worth acting on is the comment. A safety argument that survives by accident while claiming to survive by construction is what the next edit breaks — specifically, an engineer who believes the invariant holds everywhere will feel free to make the sentinel branch permit something the swap branch does not.
findings.recommendation: Two options, both cheap. report.verdict: Yes — the fix closes H-1 as claimed. Both positive-liquidity-delta call sites (StableLPManager.sol:221 via _addLiquidity, VolatileLPManager.sol:293 via _addLiquidityAt) are now unconditionally preceded by `_guardSwap(byOwner, key, true, 0, 0)`, `byOwner` is correctly threaded from `_isOwnerCall()` on all five reaching paths (Stable allocate/allocateFrom/reinvest, Volatile allocate/recenter/moveLiquidity), and `_checkSpot` compares the pool's own slot0 price symmetrically against a two-feed Chainlink cross using arithmetic I re-derived and matched against PriceDeviation.s.sol. The PoC's −22.4% moveLiquidity and −44.5% recenter drains are reduced to a bounded per-operation residual on the order of tenths of a percent. That answer would change only if a manager were wired to an `IPriceOracle` implementation that does not honour the `amountIn == 0` sentinel — the interface still does not document it (F-4) — or if the oracle's `maxSpotDeviationBps` were raised toward its 1000 bps cap to work around the availability problems in F-1.
report.verified_correct:
Guard placement and threading: every `POOL_MANAGER.modifyLiquidity` call with a positive `liquidityDelta` is preceded by the spot guard — StableLPManager.sol:215 before :221, VolatileLPManager.sol:288 before :293 — and both sit after the `getSlot0`/`PoolUninitialized` check and before `liquidityFromAmounts`, so no add can be sized at an unvouched price. `byOwner` originates at `_isOwnerCall()` in each external entry point, travels through the unlock payload, and reaches both add sites on all five paths; the owner bypass (`if (byOwner) return`, BaseLPManager.sol:355) is the only way past. Removal paths (`_pullLiquidity` in recenter/move, `claimFees` via a zero-delta poke) are correctly left ungated — removing at a skewed price is attacker-negative and gating it would add a denial surface for no benefit.

Oracle arithmetic: `_checkSpot`'s two-step `mulDiv(sqrtP,sqrtP,Q96)` → `mulDiv(priceX96, WAD*10**td0, Q96*10**td1)` pool price and `mulDiv(a0,(10**fd1)*WAD, a1*(10**fd0))` reference match `script/PriceDeviation.s.sol` expression for expression, so the repo's own "basis" measurements are directly comparable to the shipped tolerance. The split is necessary (a single-expression `sqrtP²/2^192` overflows). Zero-guards on `sqrtP`, `poolPrice` and `refPrice` all return "no opinion" rather than reverting, which the manager then fail-closes for operators only. `zeroForOne` is correctly ignored in the spot branch and the reason is documented.

M-1 and L-3: the oracle is `Ownable2Step` (transferOwnership nominates only), both tolerances are validated against `MAX_DEVIATION_CAP = 1000` in a shared setter path, and `_readBounds` resolves the underlying aggregator via `proxy.aggregator()` with every step wrapped in `try`, discarding anything outside `int128` — which correctly drops Chainlink's `2^176 − 1` "no breaker" sentinel to zero. `_read` treats an answer at or beyond a cached bound as no reference, alongside non-positive answers, zero/future timestamps and heartbeat staleness.

Sentinel safety on the swap side: no real swap can wear `amountIn == 0` on the allocate or Volatile paths — both floor the realized input at the requested amount before guarding (the one exception is F-8).

Build and suite: `forge build --sizes` reproduces the stated budgets exactly (VolatileLPManager 24,379 / 197 B, OpenVolatileLPManager 24,319 / 257 B, StableLPManager 24,117 / 459 B, ChainlinkPriceOracle 5,901 / 18,675 B, UniLens 14,532 / 10,044 B). `forge test` is green: 293 passed, 0 failed, 4 skipped (the env-gated fork tests). The Volatile side is properly pinned — two `RejectSpot` tests prove the add path reaches the sentinel branch, and test/Audit20260904SwaplessDrainPoC.t.sol drives a real `ChainlinkPriceOracle` end to end with a positive control.

Deploy plumbing: the runbook's ordering constraint (new oracle before new implementations) is correct and its rationale is accurate — master's `check` returns false on `amountIn == 0`, so the reverse order leaves operators inert. Existing EIP-1167 clones are genuinely unaffected: their add paths never consult the oracle and the swap branch of `check` is unchanged, so the new oracle is safe for them.
report.open_questions:
Whether Stable should carry the gate at all. StableLPManager's ranges are fixed at `initialize` with no setter (verified: rangeOf is written once at :78), and its operator surface has no principal-removal path — so an operator there cannot open a narrow band at a skewed price or recycle principal, and H-1's demonstrated mechanism does not reach it in the form the PoC showed. Stable's exposure is idle balance plus realized fees deployed at a bad price into a fixed range. Nobody has quantified that, and the Stable arm of the fix carries real availability and byte cost. A Stable arm of the PoC would settle it.

The basis distribution. Everything in F-1 and F-3 rests on two single-block snapshots taken 2026-07-20/21, which the analysis document itself calls too small a sample. Live re-reads attempted during this audit disagreed with each other (one lens reported Unichain ETH/UNI at 171 bps, another at 102, the repo's snapshot says 72), which is itself evidence that the quantity is volatile and that no single reading should set the parameter. Until `PriceDeviation.s.sol` is re-run over a volatile window on all four measurable chains, the correct value of `oracleMaxSpotDeviationBps` per chain is genuinely unknown — and that is exactly the step task_053 made a precondition and the runbook omits.

How often the fail-closed window actually bites. The duty cycle of a >50 bps basis on Unichain volatile pairs is unmeasured. With 24 h SVR heartbeats it could be a large fraction of the day on a trending asset, or rare. That distinction decides whether F-1 is "raise the number on one chain" or "do not run operators on those pools".

Whether a second `IPriceOracle` implementation is contemplated. F-4's fail-open branch is latent today because the only implementation is correct. It becomes live the moment anyone writes a Pyth/Redstone/second-source variant against the published interface. If the answer is "never", the natspec fix is hygiene; if "eventually", it is the difference between a documented contract and an undefined one.

Nothing was verified against live chain state in this audit — no RPC was used, and the on-chain readings quoted by earlier passes could not be reproduced. All numerical claims here trace to committed measurements in tasks/oracle_maxdeviation_analysis.md.
